subject: Critical Thinking
title: Why Smart People Fall for Biases Too
description: One-minute skill: Why Smart People Fall for Biases Too.

hook.text: Higher IQ doesn't protect against cognitive biases. In some cases, it actually makes them worse.

buildup.text: The 'bias blind spot' — people believe they're less biased than average. Smarter people believe this more strongly.

discovery.text: Intelligence gives you better tools for rationalizing — constructing clever arguments for conclusions you already want.

twist.text: West, Meserve & Stanovich (2012) found that smarter people are better at spotting others' biases — not their own.

climax.text: Intellectual humility — admitting you're probably wrong — is the only consistent debiaser across IQ levels.

punchline.text: Smart doesn't mean unbiased. It means better at hiding it.

quiz.question: What is the 'bias blind spot'?
options: Inability to see in the dark
Believing you're less biased than you actually are
A bias that only affects experts

details.summary: Intelligence does not protect against cognitive biases. In fact, smarter people are often better at rationalizing their biased conclusions, making them harder to correct. The bias blind spot affects everyone.
details.whyItMatters: Believing you are too smart for biases is itself a bias. Intellectual humility is the real defense against systematic thinking errors.
takeaways: High IQ correlates with better rationalization, not less bias
The bias blind spot makes people see biases in others but not themselves
Debiasing requires structured methods, not just intelligence

faq.question: Why does higher intelligence sometimes make biases worse?
faq.answer: Intelligent people are better at constructing convincing arguments for conclusions they reached emotionally. This skill makes their biased reasoning more persuasive to themselves and others.

faq.question: What is the bias blind spot and how can you overcome it?
faq.answer: The bias blind spot is the tendency to recognize biases in others while believing you are immune. Overcoming it requires feedback from others, structured decision processes, and genuine intellectual humility.
